<reason>Both sides argued the motion as written and avoided fake sourcing, and both were rhetorically sharp. PRO built a coherent moral frame (an unpaid junior post is an unpaid job whose price is unpaid time; the state should not license that market) and answered the pressure questions directly with clean A1/A2 labels. But CON controlled the decisive comparison and kept generating dilemmas PRO could only partly absorb. Three CON pressures mattered most: (1) the conversion burden — PRO's case only benefits anyone if the banned post reappears as a paid one, and PRO's answer ("if it only exists because it can be extracted free, its disappearance is no social loss") was fairly exposed as an unverifiable article of faith about every thin-budget host; (2) the pincer at [B2.2]/[B4.4], where PRO's own concessions (the person who can take three unpaid weeks "already has housing or savings"; the uncushioned "was never walking through" the door) were turned into "a demolition with no beneficiary" — PRO's continuum reply and late naming of a beneficiary in closing were reasonable but re-collapsed into the unproven conversion; (3) the exemption dilemma — credential-gated (excludes the retrainee, the non-graduate) versus vague purpose test (chilling small charities). PRO's shift to a functional test (duration, substitution for staff, later credential use) was the best available answer and blunted the volunteering-swallow objection, but CON's chilling-effect point survived. PRO also missed two available turns: CON conceded caps, means-testing, supervision standards and enforcement of existing wage law, which are themselves restrictions — PRO gestured at this ("décor on extraction") without pressing it. CON's private-door frame ("regulate what you can reach; don't abolish it and call the remaining darkness equality") and closing image about sawing off the bottom rung made the choice easier to decide.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.2]/[B4.4] pincer: PRO cannot claim both that the ban ends an exclusionary filter and that the working-class applicant "was never walking through" the door. Combined with PRO's concession that anyone able to take three unpaid weeks "already has housing or savings," CON crystallised the case as taking from the cushioned while giving nothing to the uncushioned unless the unproven conversion to paid posts occurs — a loop PRO's closing beneficiary claim reopened rather than closed.</best_rebuttal>
